name: Erik Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms or government. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43, teach five beginner hand-drum pupils at the youth club, clean up basic recordings and play a café set when it is booked. I left school after secondary classes and still ask the lead engineer to check my hard edits.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part feels good, and what is hard to carry home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A quiet child finding the shared beat feels like a good afternoon. My partner works at the library, and our two school-age children and mortgage mean I check the paid club blocks before agreeing to a new set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the youth club that AI Plateau makes my booking list and rough mixes quicker, but the children still have to hold a beat together. I would keep the Friday hand-drum circle as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day to label takes and plan practice, though I check the rhythm against the original audio. My partner’s library pay is steady and we have four months of expenses saved, so one missed session would not threaten the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my five beginner pupils and the two paid club recording blocks next month. This week I’d ask the club for written session dates before my partner swaps a library shift for school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about my own job and income. A quieter edit afternoon would leave time to practise, not force a bill to go unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a missed block cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A missed recording block would cost less than a month of mortgage payments. I would still want the club to tell me early so we can plan pickup for our two children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust the AI labels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not let a neat AI label decide which take a pupil hears. The sound of the wrong beat is still the wrong beat, however tidy the file looks.

I would accept quicker **booking lists** while checking the original recordings.

AI **labels** help me work but cannot tell whether the rhythm feels right.

feel: I feel **calm** about one quiet edit afternoon and the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the club Steady Disruption may make basic track cleaning and parent messages cheap, and we should put actual paid hours on paper. I would still run the drum circle while families book it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Track cleanup is about a third of my pay, and I am still junior at the harder work. The club may keep its lead engineer and cut my blocks first, which would make our mortgage budget tighter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the club this month for its next term’s paid editing hours. If one of two monthly blocks disappears in the first year, I’d ask its lead engineer to approve a sample and stay for my first check with the new AI stem-separation tool, which splits a recording into separate parts. I’d add a second group lesson only if a room is open and six paying families cover hire and my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious because my own hours could shrink, though four months saved lets me test one change. I cannot send my family a forecast instead of a pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to try that audio tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lead engineer would have to approve the sample and stay for the first check. I use AI for labels already, but I have never learned how to split a recording into separate parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many families make another lesson pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six fees at our current price would pay the room and my afternoon. If only five families sign, I would keep the first group and leave the extra afternoon empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the club AGI by 2028 could do track cleanup and lesson planning as well as a person for less. Capable robots for hands-on playing would follow around 2031, so I would separate recording work from the live circle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my editing blocks to shrink in 2028, while the hand-drum lessons may still pay for a while. Four months of savings and my partner’s library wage buy some time, but not a long mortgage gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the club now for a six-month paid block schedule and the library whether a part-time stockroom vacancy is actually posted. In the first year after 2028, if both editing blocks end, I’d apply only if the written pay after travel replaces lost club income and keep pupils until an offer arrives. I’d ask the lender about temporary terms only if our reserve falls below one month, and read the whole-loan cost before signing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious rather than helpless, because the library and lessons are real places I can ask. I would be alarmed if the club cut the teaching circle too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the library definitely hire you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The stockroom job would need an actual vacancy and a rate in writing. My partner works at the library. A family connection is not a posted job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask what the shorter mortgage payments cost over the whole loan before signing anything. Four months saved buys time to read the terms, not permission to ignore them.

I would keep the **live circle** while parents still pay for it.

do: Check the **club schedule** and whether a library stockroom vacancy is posted now; keep pupils until a paid offer.
Apply in the first year after **2028** only if both blocks end and written pay after travel replaces club income.
Ask the **lender** about whole-loan hardship costs only if savings fall below one month; sign only after reading terms.
feel: I feel **anxious** about editing loss, with conditional alarm if lessons fall too.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **2028 screen work** from capable robots for hands-on playing around 2031.
A library move requires a **posted vacancy** and enough net pay; lender help waits until the reserve shrinks.
S2.quote: A family connection is not a posted job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the club AGI by 2031 gives us five years to build paid skills before track editing changes. Robots able to do hands-on playing as well as people would follow around 2034, so I would still ask for written live dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn to run a school rhythm group properly instead of relying on one-to-one beginners, but I am no expert yet. A course has to fit the children’s pickups and cannot use the mortgage account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the community college next term about a short group-teaching course, but enroll only if a grant pays the fee, my partner can cover pickups and classes do not replace paid club hours. If qualified and a posted school music-aide vacancy pays enough after travel and childcare, I’d apply before 2031. In the first year after AGI, I’d keep my club circle until a paid school offer covers travel and lost club income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about the editing income, yet five years gives me a way to test a new skill. I would not call a certificate a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the course fit your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children leave school at different times on Wednesdays. My partner could cover pickup only on an early library shift, so I would check the rota before enrolling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the certificate guarantee work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the school whether it accepts the college certificate and what a paid aide hour is worth. Without a vacancy at a usable rate, I would stay with the club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the club AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to make a better plan, with capable robots for hands-on playing around 2039. I would still put next month’s paid blocks on the calendar first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might have a school post and a stronger savings account, if I qualify and a vacancy comes through. Today’s four-month reserve makes the mortgage manageable, but it is not a reason to buy a room full of equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my five pupils and paid editing blocks this year, and set aside fifteen from each paid café set after the mortgage payment clears. In the first year after 2036, I’d take school aide hours only if I qualify and a posted paid offer covers travel and childcare, while keeping club lessons until the school work is certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be uneasy about the far date rather than frightened this year. The family can plan while my partner’s library pay and my club hours continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you put aside now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fifteen comes from a paid set, not a promised one. I want another month of bills saved before I even dream of renting a studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children they may love music without making it their only plan. They can watch me ask for a real wage before I change jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the editing blocks could end before a school role is open. A written club schedule, a real paid vacancy and clear mortgage hardship terms would help me keep the household steady.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask how I decide when an AI stem-separation tool is safe. I would test an AI stem-separation tool on my own recording and ask permission before using any pupil’s track.

headlineQuote: I would test an AI stem-separation tool on my own recording and ask permission before using any pupil’s track.
portrait: At **43**, Erik teaches hand drums, edits basic club recordings and plays paid café sets after secondary school.
His typical **pay**, partner’s library work and four-month reserve give the family some room to adjust.
He uses AI **daily** for labels and plans, and learns new audio tools only with approved material.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens junior editing blocks first; a funded course and genuine school vacancy shape his response.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end paid editing blocks before a school role opens.
whatWouldHelp: A written **club schedule**, paid vacancy and clear lender terms would help him protect the mortgage.
